title: Domain-Driven Design & Clean Architecture
summary: Model the code around the business, and keep the business rules from ever learning that a database exists. Software stays soft for a decade instead of rotting in two years.

blocks.markdown:
Model the software around the *business*, and keep the rules isolated from frameworks and databases.

- **DDD** shapes code around real business concepts using the experts' own words — a **ubiquitous language**.
- **Clean / Hexagonal / Onion** are three names for one rule: business rules sit in the center, tech lives at the edges, dependencies point **inward**.
- The payoff is **testability and changeability**: test logic with no DB, swap Postgres for DynamoDB without touching a rule.
- The cost is **ceremony** — more files, more indirection. Overkill for CRUD, essential for a complex domain.

blocks.subTitle: When to reach for it
blocks.markdown:
Match the investment to the domain's real complexity.

| Situation | Reach for |
|---|---|
| Simple CRUD, thin logic | Plain layered app |
| Rich business rules | Tactical DDD |
| Many teams, big system | Strategic DDD + contexts |
| Need to swap DB freely | Clean / Hexagonal |
| Throwaway prototype | None — just ship |

blocks.subTitle: Ubiquitous language
blocks.markdown:
The hardest-to-replace part of business software is the **model of the domain** — the concepts and rules.

- Engineers and experts must share **one precise vocabulary**, identical in conversation and in class names.
- If an expert says "an order can't ship until payment clears," that should map almost word-for-word onto code.
- Most defects come from **translation loss** between what experts mean and what engineers build.
- The language is enforced **per bounded context** — one word, one meaning, inside that boundary.

blocks.subTitle: Strategic DDD: bounded contexts
blocks.markdown:
A **bounded context** is a boundary inside which a model and its words mean exactly one thing.

- One giant shared model collapses: Billing cares about payment method, Shipping about address. Forcing both into one `Customer` makes a monster.
- Inside Sales, "Order" is a cart being assembled; inside Shipping it's a parcel with a tracking number. Same word, different model — and that's fine.
- The **context map** charts all contexts and how they relate (Shared Kernel, Customer-Supplier, Conformist, Anti-Corruption Layer).
- Contexts are also the natural seams for splitting a monolith into services ([b16-monolith-microservices](b16-monolith-microservices.md)).

blocks.subTitle: Tactical DDD: the building blocks
blocks.markdown:
Inside one context, DDD gives you a vocabulary of object types.

- **Entity** — distinct identity that persists through change; compared by ID (a `User`).
- **Value object** — defined only by its values, immutable, compared by value (`Money`). You replace it, never edit it.
- **Aggregate** — a cluster of objects loaded and saved as one consistency unit (`Order` plus its `OrderLine`s).
- **Repository** — a collection-like interface for loading and saving aggregates.
- **Domain service** — logic that fits no single entity (a transfer touching two accounts).
- **Domain event** — a past-tense record that something happened (`OrderPlaced`).

blocks.subTitle: Aggregate roots & invariants
blocks.markdown:
The **aggregate root** is the only legal entry point — all changes go through it, so it enforces invariants.

```python
class Order:                      # aggregate root
    def __init__(self, id, customer_id):
        self.lines, self.status = [], "DRAFT"

    def add_line(self, line):
        if self.status != "DRAFT":
            raise OrderAlreadyPlaced   # invariant
        self.lines.append(line)

    def place(self):
        if not self.lines:
            raise EmptyOrder           # invariant
        self.status = "PLACED"
        return OrderPlaced(self.id)    # domain event
```

- Outside code holds a reference to `Order`, never to an `OrderLine` directly.
- Illegal states are **impossible to construct** — the only way in is these methods.

blocks.subTitle: The dependency rule
blocks.markdown:
Clean, Hexagonal, and Onion all enforce one law: **source-code dependencies point only inward**, toward business rules.

- The center (entities) knows nothing about the outside; outer layers (DB, web, framework) depend on inner ones.
- Frameworks and databases change far more often — and are far slower to test against — than core rules.
- So you invert: make the volatile, slow, external stuff depend on the stable, fast, internal rules — never the reverse.
- That single rule is the seed all three architectures grow from.

blocks.subTitle: Ports & adapters
blocks.markdown:
How does the database depend on the domain when the domain needs to save things? You **invert** it.

- The domain defines an interface — a **port** like `OrderRepository`. The domain calls that interface.
- The outside supplies an **adapter** — `PostgresOrderRepository` *implements* the port.
- At compile time the adapter imports the domain; the domain imports nothing back. At runtime you inject the implementation.
- **Driving adapters** (REST, CLI, tests) push requests in; **driven adapters** (Postgres, Kafka, email) are reached out to. Swap any adapter without touching the core.

blocks.subTitle: What you're trading
blocks.markdown:
Isolation buys speed and safety; it costs ceremony and indirection.

| Axis | Isolate when | Skip when |
|---|---|---|
| Ceremony | Rich, growing rules | Thin CRUD |
| Indirection | Infra will change | DB is fixed |
| Consistency | Must agree atomically | Eventual is fine |

Every call crossing a port also means a mapping step: domain object to DB row to DTO.

blocks.subTitle: Keep aggregates small
blocks.markdown:
Small aggregates scale; big ones cause lock contention and giant transactions.

- **Reference other aggregates by ID**, not by embedded object.
- **Change only one aggregate per transaction** — keeps the boundary tight and loads independent.
- Cross-aggregate consistency becomes **eventual**, carried by domain events ([b17-event-driven-cqrs](b17-event-driven-cqrs.md)).
- If two pieces of data must always agree atomically, keep them in **one** aggregate instead.

blocks.subTitle: Real systems
blocks.markdown:
These ideas run at organizational scale.

- **Amazon** split its monolith into service-per-team — each service is effectively a bounded context with its own data and model.
- **Netflix** integrates playback, billing, and recommendations through **domain events** on a streaming backbone, not shared databases.
- **Spring / .NET DI** make ports-and-adapters cheap — the framework lives at the outer ring and injects implementations inward.
- **Banking ledgers** are the textbook home: `Money` refuses invalid arithmetic, an `Account` root enforces "balance never negative."

blocks.subTitle: Signals it's working
blocks.markdown:
This is a design philosophy, so watch for observable signs it pays off.

- **Domain tests run with no infrastructure** — fast in-memory units (~1–5 ms), not DB containers (100–1000x slower).
- **Swapping infra touches one file** — one new adapter, one wiring change, zero ripple into rules.
- **Domain classes import nothing from frameworks** — grep for `org.springframework` or SQL and find zero hits.
- **Code uses the business's words** — if experts say "settlement" and code says `process_record_2`, the language broke down.
- **Teams ship independently** — frequent "your change broke us" means leaky boundaries.

The mistakes that bite in interviews and production:

- **"Clean means no framework."** No — the framework lives at the *edge*, injected through ports. You still use Spring.
- **Anemic domain model.** Entities as data bags with all logic in service classes — procedural code in OO clothes.
- **One giant aggregate.** A huge `Customer` holding orders, addresses, and history becomes a contention hotspot.
- **Entity vs value object mix-up.** Giving `Money` an ID, or comparing `Address` by reference. Ask: does identity matter?
- **Repositories that leak the DB.** Returning ORM entities with lazy relations means the database leaked inward.
